faqs.q: What should I include on an HVAC invoice?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business name and license number, the client and service address, a dated line-item list (service call, labor, each repair, parts), tax, and a total due. Split labor and parts so warranty terms are easy to reference.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate tax automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantity and rate per line, and the subtotal, tax and total update automatically. Leave the tax rate blank if you are not required to charge sales tax.

faqs.q: Do you have an HVAC invoice example I can see?
faqs.a: Yes. This HVAC invoice template comes pre-filled with sample line items (service call, AC tune-up, capacitor replacement, refrigerant recharge) at typical rates - use it as an example to see how a completed HVAC invoice should look, then replace the sample items with your own.

deepDive.heading: HVAC invoicing in practice: licenses, refrigerant rules and the parts-labor tax split
deepDive.sub: How working HVAC contractors structure invoices so they pass board scrutiny, warranty claims and sales tax audits at the same time.

blocks.h3: Contractor license and EPA numbers on the invoice
paras: HVAC work sits under state contractor boards — CSLT license numbers in California, TACLA in Texas, MHIC in Maryland, and equivalents elsewhere — and most boards expect the license number on any document you hand a customer that requests payment. Beyond the state license, refrigerant handling falls under EPA Section 608: any technician opening a charged system should be 608-certified, and many companies print the company's EPA registration alongside the state license on invoices that include refrigerant work.
This template's header carries both a License # and an EIN / Tax ID field. Operators who do refrigerant work commonly add a line for the EPA cert in the notes field of their master copy.

blocks.h3: Split labor and parts — the tax and warranty both depend on it
paras: A single 'AC repair — $425' line is the weakest way to bill HVAC work. Most states tax parts and materials differently from labor: Texas taxes parts but generally not residential repair labor; New York exempts commercial installation labor but not parts; many states tax everything on a residential repair invoice. When labor and parts share one line, you cannot apply the correct rate to each — and at audit time you have no record of which portion was which.

Splitting them also keeps warranties clean. Manufacturer parts warranties typically run 1–10 years while the installing contractor's labor warranty is usually 90 days to 1 year. Separate lines let the customer see exactly what falls under which guarantee — this template's default notes field ('Labor guaranteed for 90 days; manufacturer warranty applies to parts and equipment') references that split directly.

blocks.h3: Billing the service call fee, tune-ups and maintenance plans
paras: The three most common HVAC billing patterns each get their own line treatment:
list: Diagnostic / service call fee: a flat charge for coming out and finding the problem. Some companies waive it when the customer approves the repair on the spot — if that's your policy, show the fee with a matching discount line so the customer sees the value instead of wondering if they were never charged.
Tune-up / seasonal maintenance: flat-rate per system, usually billed at completion. Two-system households get two lines — customers dispute combined 'multi-system' charges far more often.

Maintenance plan invoicing: reference the plan name and visit number, like a subscription. Most plans bill annually or semi-annually in advance; the invoice should show the coverage window (e.g., 'two precision tune-ups, priority scheduling, 15% off repairs') so renewals sell themselves.

blocks.h3: Invoicing refrigerant correctly after the 2025 transition
paras: Refrigerant line items deserve precision. Since the R-410A phase-down began under the AIM Act, per-pound pricing moved to a new R-454B and R-32 era on new equipment, and recovery/recharge work on older R-22 and R-410A systems still appears on plenty of invoices. Best practice is to bill refrigerant by the pound with the type spelled out ('R-410A recharge, 2.5 lb'), because the per-pound rates differ sharply by type and customers compare invoices across companies.

Also note: several states tax refrigerant as tangible parts while treating the recharge labor as a service. Keeping the pounds on their own line lets you apply the right rate to the material and the right rate to the labor.

blocks.h3: Warranty and callback work still needs an invoice
paras: Zero-dollar invoices for warranty callbacks are worth issuing, not skipping. A $0 invoice documents what failed, what was replaced, and that no charge applied under the labor guarantee — which matters when the customer later disputes a related repair or asks for the service history at home-sale time. Print the original invoice number in the reference field so the callback ties to the job it answers.

For manufacturer-warranty parts claims you will typically need the model and serial numbers of both the failed and replacement components on paperwork — adding those to the line item description ('Condenser fan motor — Trane 4TTR6036, S/N 24192K1LF → replacement OEM motor') makes claim filing painless.
